blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights Ambry, LinkedIn's scalable geo-distributed object store, as a robust solution for handling the massive scale of modern social networks. The paper emphasizes Ambry's ability to efficiently manage read-heavy workloads (over 95% of traffic) for immutable blobs, ranging from small files to large media objects, with high throughput (up to 88% of network bandwidth) and low latency (under 50ms for 1MB blobs). Key design choices include a multi-master architecture with configurable consistency levels (similar to Cassandra), asynchronous replication across datacenters, and a partitioning scheme that decouples logical and physical data placement to enable transparent rebalancing. The system also employs load balancing techniques to mitigate hotspots, achieving significant reductions in request rate and disk usage imbalance (6-10x and 9-10x, respectively). The blog praises Ambry's production readiness, having operated across four datacenters for over two years, and its innovative approaches to handling large blobs via chunking and append-only logs.
paper_title: Ambry: LinkedIn's scalable geo-distributed object store
paper_abstract: The infrastructure beneath a worldwide social network has to continually serve billions of variable-sized media objects such as photos, videos, and audio clips. These objects must be stored and served with low latency and high throughput by a system that is geo-distributed, highly scalable, and load-balanced. Existing file systems and object stores face several challenges when serving such large objects. We present Ambry, a production-quality system for storing large immutable data (called blobs). Ambry is designed in a decentralized way and leverages techniques such as logical blob grouping, asynchronous replication, rebalancing mechanisms, zero-cost failure detection, and OS caching. Ambry has been running in LinkedIn’s production environment for the past 2 years, serving up to 10K requests per second across more than 400 million users. Our experimental evaluation reveals that Ambry offers high efficiency (utilizing up to 88% of the network bandwidth), low latency (less than 50 ms latency for a 1 MB object), and load balancing (improving imbalance of request rate among disks by 8x-10x).

figures.title: Ambry system architecture
figures.caption: The overall architecture of Ambry is shown in Figure 1. The system is composed of three main components: Frontends that receive and route requests, Datanodes that store the actual data, and Cluster Managers that maintain the state of the cluster.
